title: Integrating AI in College Education: Positive yet Mixed Experiences with ChatGPT
extended_summary:
This paper examines how ChatGPT can be integrated into higher education and what kinds of benefits and concerns emerge when students use it in an actual course. The authors focus on a central question: whether a generative AI chatbot can function as a useful teaching assistant in a college medical imaging course, while also identifying students’ attitudes, usage patterns, and concerns about reliability and educational value.

The intervention was a customized ChatGPT-4 Turbo teaching application called ChatGe, developed for an undergraduate medical imaging course. The study compared use of standard ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-4 Turbo, and two versions of the customized course-specific tool (ChatGe-V1 and ChatGe-V2). Across a Spring 2024 semester, the researchers collected multiple forms of data: student questionnaires about usage and perceptions, comparative evaluations of answers generated by human TAs versus chatbot systems, and student exam grades. The app was used to support clarification of course content, homework, and programming-related tasks, and the customized system was iteratively improved using student feedback.

Participants were students enrolled in two sections of the same undergraduate medical imaging course at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute in the United States, taught by two instructors who shared syllabus, textbook, and exam questions. The course context was a college classroom setting with some MATLAB sessions. The paper also reports that instructor framing mattered: in the section where ChatGPT was actively encouraged, adoption was much higher than in the section where the instructor emphasized caution.

The main conclusions are that students’ experiences with ChatGPT were positive overall but mixed. Students valued convenience, interactivity, and help with understanding course material, but many remained concerned about trustworthiness and answer accuracy. The original general-purpose ChatGPT-4 outperformed the first custom version, but the improved custom tool, ChatGe-V2, became comparable to or better than ChatGPT-4 and even human TAs on some student preference measures. The authors conclude that AI chatbots can be useful educational assistants and reduce TA workload, but successful implementation requires better course-specific customization, clear usage guidelines, and attention to student trust and instructor messaging.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's ChatGPT family of large language model chatbots used for conversational question answering, explanation, and content support.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in an undergraduate medical imaging course as ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4 Turbo for course-content clarification, programming/homework help, comparative answer generation versus human TAs, and as the base platform for the customized course chatbot ChatGe.

findings.finding_summary: Student survey results indicated generally positive perceptions of ChatGPT use in the course, with about 65.15% of students using ChatGPT models. Nearly all users reported using the chatbots for clarification of course content, and over half used them for programming and homework; however, students also expressed limited confidence in response accuracy, and among non-users 63.15% reported not using ChatGPT because they did not trust it.
findings.measure: Student survey on usage, perceived helpfulness, and trust/confidence

findings.finding_summary: In comparative course Q&A evaluations, the original ChatGPT-4 performed better than the first customized version (ChatGe-V1), but the improved customized version (ChatGe-V2) was comparable to or better than ChatGPT-4 Turbo and even human TAs on student preference voting. The paper reports a statistically significant difference by prior ChatGPT use: students who had used ChatGPT statistically preferred ChatGe-V2 (p-value = 0.091 from Chi-squared test), while no statistically significant preference was found among non-users.
findings.measure: Student preference votes on AI- versus TA-generated answers to course questions

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatGPT-based systems generated answers instantly, compared with 15–20 minutes for human TAs. TAs also found that ChatGPT could generate MATLAB programming demonstrations as effectively as they could, suggesting potential workload reduction for instructional support.
findings.measure: TA time required to generate answers and programming demonstrations

findings.finding_summary: Adoption of ChatGPT varied substantially by instructor framing: usage was 87.5% in the section where the instructor actively promoted ChatGPT, versus 38.2% in the section where the instructor emphasized caution. This suggests implementation messaging materially affected uptake, while concerns about accuracy remained a major barrier.
findings.measure: Section-level adoption rates from post-exam survey

identified_tools.name: ChatGe
identified_tools.description: A customized ChatGPT-based teaching application for a college medical imaging course, built on ChatGPT-4 Turbo and tailored with course materials and prompting.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as a specialized chatbot (ChatGe-V1 and ChatGe-V2) to answer course-related student questions, support understanding of medical imaging theory, and compare its answers against ChatGPT and human TAs.

findings.finding_summary: Student survey responses were generally positive toward chatbot use, but students did not rate ChatGe-V1 as significantly better than ChatGPT-4 Turbo on the 5-point questionnaire. This negative comparative feedback motivated the authors to revise the system into ChatGe-V2 with more course-related materials and more specific prompts.
findings.measure: 5-point student survey comparing chatbot usefulness and quality

findings.finding_summary: After revision, ChatGe-V2 improved over ChatGe-V1 and was reported as comparable to or better than ChatGPT-4 Turbo, ChatGe-V1, and even human TAs in student preference voting on seven selected course questions. Students who had used ChatGPT for the course statistically preferred ChatGe-V2 (p-value = 0.091 from Chi-squared test), whereas no statistically significant preference was found among non-users.
findings.measure: Student preference votes on responses to course content questions

findings.finding_summary: ChatGe-V2 was reported to generate answers instantly, whereas human TAs required 15–20 minutes. The system could also infer intended meaning even when student questions were erroneous, indicating practical efficiency advantages for course support.
findings.measure: Response generation time and handling of erroneous student questions

quality_tier_rationale: This is a semester-long empirical classroom study with surveys, preference voting, and descriptive comparisons, but it does not present a randomized or strong quasi-experimental design for learning outcomes. Reported evidence is primarily perceptual, correlational, and operational rather than causal.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive perceived usefulness, higher adoption under supportive implementation, and operational efficiency gains, but learning outcome effects are mixed and no standardized effect sizes are reported. Overall impact appears promising but unclear in magnitude.
